steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has had some success recently in several applications, from video games to robotics, but there are several shortcomings that get in the way of using RL in the real world. One of them is sample efficiency. In a simulated environment it is possible to collect millions of data points, but in the real world it is just not feasible to do that. This inefficiency gets even worse when one agent has to solve multiple tasks, which is what we would expect of a generally intelligent agent.

One way to overcome this is to reuse behaviours that were already learned to solve new tasks, ideally without any more learning. This approach is often compositional, meaning that the agent first learns individual skills and then combines them to get new behaviours. In the literature there are several notions of compositionality. One is spatial composition, where skills are combined into a new single behaviour that is executed to achieve sets of high-level goals ("pick up an object that is both blue and a box"). Another is temporal composition, where sub-skills are called one after another to achieve sequences of high-level goals (for example, "pickup a blue object and then a box").

Spatial composition is usually done with a weighted combination of learned successor features. Notably, other work has shown spatial composition with Boolean operators such as negation and conjunction, which gives semantically meaningful behaviours without further learning. Agents can then use this ability to follow natural language instructions.

- Temporal composition
  - learn options for sub-goals of temporal logic tasks + high-level policy over options; reuse options in new tasks (cite)
  - end-to-end neural architectures learning sub-skills from training set, generalise to similar tasks (cite)
- Gap
  - prior work (cite): some options can't transfer to new tasks; gives method to detect when
  - example: "getting blue objects" + "getting boxes" -> "pickup a blue object and then a box" works, "pickup a blue object that is not a box, and then a box that is not blue" doesn't
  - cause: compositions strictly temporal or strictly spatial
  - spatial alone not enough for long-horizon tasks: long action sequence before learning signal (cite)
- Our approach and contributions
  - zero-shot spatial + temporal composition; temporal logic, e.g. LTL (cite); chain/order skills, conditions always or never met
  - (1) skill machines: FSMs, Boolean compositions of skill primitives, built from regular language spec
  - (2) zero/few-shot via reward machines (cite); SMs satisficing; off-policy RL for optimality; no new assumption
  - (3) results: video game + continuous control; near-optimal to optimal without further learning; beats baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has had some success recently in several applications, from video games to robotics, but there are several shortcomings that get in the way of using RL in the real world. One of them is sample efficiency. In a simulated environment it is possible to collect millions of data points, but in the real world it is just not feasible to do that. This inefficiency gets even worse when one agent has to solve multiple tasks, which is what we would expect of a generally intelligent agent.

One way to overcome this is to reuse behaviours that were already learned to solve new tasks, ideally without any more learning. This approach is often compositional, meaning that the agent first learns individual skills and then combines them to get new behaviours. In the literature there are several notions of compositionality. One is spatial composition, where skills are combined into a new single behaviour that is executed to achieve sets of high-level goals ("pick up an object that is both blue and a box"). Another is temporal composition, where sub-skills are called one after another to achieve sequences of high-level goals (for example, "pickup a blue object and then a box").

Spatial composition is usually done with a weighted combination of learned successor features. Notably, other work has shown spatial composition with Boolean operators such as negation and conjunction, which gives semantically meaningful behaviours without further learning. Agents can then use this ability to follow natural language instructions.

For temporal composition, one of the most common approaches is to learn options for the sub-goals in temporal logic tasks, and at the same time learn a high-level policy over the options which actually solves the task, and then reuse the learned options in new tasks. But other works have instead proposed end-to-end neural network architectures that learn sub-skills from a training set and can generalise to similar new tasks.

Another work observes that in all these prior works, some of the sub-skills (e.g., options) learned from previous tasks cannot be transferred well to new tasks, and they give a method to determine when this happens. For example, if the agent already learned one option for "getting blue objects" and another one for "getting boxes", it can reuse them to "pickup a blue object and then a box", but it cannot reuse them to "pickup a blue object that is not a box, and then a box that is not blue". We can see that this problem happens because all the compositions in prior works are either strictly temporal or strictly spatial. The example shows that temporal composition alone is not enough, but spatial composition is also not enough to solve long-horizon tasks. In these cases it is often almost impossible for the agent to learn, because there is a large sequence of actions that has to be executed before the agent gets a learning signal.

So this work tries to address this problem by combining the approaches above into an agent that can do both zero-shot spatial and zero-shot temporal composition. We focus in particular on temporal logic composition, like linear temporal logic (LTL), which lets agents chain and order their skills in sequence while making sure some conditions are always or never met. Our main contributions are the following:

- 1. Skill machines: We propose skill machines (SM). These are finite state machines (FSM) that encode the solution to any task specified with any given regular language (such as regular fragments of LTL) as a series of Boolean compositions of skill primitives, which are composable sub-skills for achieving high-level goals in the environment. An SM is defined by translating the regular language task specification into an FSM, and then defining the skill to use in each FSM state as a Boolean composition of pretrained skill primitives.

- 2. Zero-shot and few-shot learning using skill machines: We use reward machines (RM), which are finite state machines that encode the reward structure of a task, to show how an SM can be obtained directly from an LTL task specification. We prove that these SMs are satisficing, meaning that given a task specification and regular reachability assumptions, an agent can solve the task successfully while adhering to any constraints. We also show how standard off-policy RL algorithms can be used to improve the resulting behaviours when we want optimality. This needs no new assumption in RL.

- 3. Empirical and qualitative results: We demonstrate our approach in several environments, including a high-dimensional video game and a continuous control environment. The results show that our method can produce near-optimal to optimal behaviour for a variety of long-horizon tasks without further learning, and the empirical results far surpass all the representative state-of-the-art baselines.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
While reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved recent success in several applications, ranging from video games [1] to robotics [2], several shortcomings still hinder RL's real-world applicability. One issue is sample efficiency—while it is possible to collect millions of data points in a simulated environment, it is simply not feasible to do so in the real world. This inefficiency is made worse when a single agent is required to solve multiple tasks, as we would expect of a generally intelligent agent.

One approach to overcoming this challenge is to reuse learned behaviours to solve new tasks [3], preferably without further learning. Such an approach is often compositional — an agent first learns individual skills and then combines them to produce novel behaviours. The literature contains several notions of compositionality, such as spatial composition [4,5], where skills are combined to produce a new single behaviour to be executed to achieve sets of high-level goals ("pick up an object that is both blue and a box"), and temporal composition [6,7], where sub-skills are invoked one after the other to achieve sequences of high-level goals (for example, "pickup a blue object and then a box").

Spatial composition is commonly achieved through a weighted combination of learned successor features [8,9,10]. Notably, work by [11,12] has demonstrated spatial composition using Boolean operators, such as negation and conjunction, producing semantically meaningful behaviours without further learning. Agents can then leverage this ability to follow natural language instructions [13,14].

One of the most common approaches to temporal composition is to learn options for achieving the sub-goals present in temporal logic tasks while learning a high-level policy over the options to actually solve the task, and then to reuse the learned options in new tasks [15,16]. However, other works like [17] have proposed end-to-end neural network architectures for learning sub-skills from a training set that can generalise to similar new tasks.

⟨11⟩ observe that for all these prior works, some of the sub-skills (e.g., options) learned from previous tasks cannot be transferred satisfactorily to new tasks, and they provide a method to determine when this is the case. For example, if the agent has previously learned an option for "getting blue objects" and another for "getting boxes", it can reuse them to "pickup a blue object and then a box", but it cannot reuse them to "pickup a blue object that is not a box, and then a box that is not blue". We can observe that this problem arises because all the compositions in prior works are either strictly temporal or strictly spatial. While the example shows that temporal composition alone is insufficient, spatial composition is also not enough for solving long-horizon tasks. In these instances, it is often near impossible for the agent to learn, owing to the large sequence of actions that must be executed before a learning signal is received [19].

Hence, this work aims to address the highlighted problem by combining the approaches above to develop an agent capable of both zero-shot spatial and temporal composition. We focus in particular on temporal logic composition, such as linear temporal logic (LTL) [20], which allows agents to sequentially chain and order their skills while ensuring certain conditions are always or never met. We make the following main contributions:

- 1. Skill machines: We propose skill machines (SM), which are finite state machines (FSM) that encode the solution to any task specified using any given regular language (such as regular fragments of LTL) as a series of Boolean compositions of skill primitives —composable sub-skills for achieving high-level goals in the environment. An SM is defined by translating the regular language task specification into an FSM, and defining the skill to use in each FSM state as a Boolean composition of pretrained skill primitives.

- 2. Zero-shot and few-shot learning using skill machines: By leveraging reward machines (RM) [21] —finite state machines that encode the reward structure of a task—we show how an SM can be obtained directly from an LTL task specification, and we prove that these SMs are satisficing —given a task specification and regular reachability assumptions, an agent can successfully solve the task while adhering to any constraints. We further show how standard off-policy RL algorithms can be used to improve the resulting behaviours when optimality is desired. This requires no new assumption in RL.

- 3. Empirical and qualitative results: We demonstrate our approach in several environments, including a high-dimensional video game and a continuous control environment. Our results indicate that our method can produce near-optimal to optimal behaviour for a variety of long-horizon tasks without further learning, with empirical results that far surpass all the representative state-of-the-art baselines.
